screening.reason: Includes an ABIDE resting-state fMRI connectivity analysis (one of four disorder datasets studied) comparing unsupervised connectivity-based clusters to clinical ASD diagnostic groups (Inclusion 2, 3)

evidence_spans.text:
Four hundred and ﬁfty-four subjects with complete phenotypic
data were selected from the Autism Brain Imaging Data
Exchange (ABIDE) database (http://fcon_1000.projects.nitrc.
org/indi/abide/index.html). The sample consisted of 256 HC, 166
subjects with autism, and 32 subjects with Asperger’s.
evidence_spans.claim: ABIDE cohort: 454 subjects with complete phenotypic data (256 HC, 166 autism, 32 Asperger’s); PDD-NOS excluded.

evidence_spans.text:
Each subject was scanned at
one of the following seven diﬀerent sites: California Institute of
Technology (Caltech), Carnegie Mellon University (CMU), NYU
Langone Medical Center (NYU), University of Pittsburgh School
of Medicine (Pitt), San Diego State University (SDSU), Trinity
Center for Health Sciences (Trinity), and University of California
Los Angeles (UCLA).
evidence_spans.claim: ABIDE cohort was drawn from seven sites.

evidence_spans.text:
For most of the sites, diagnosis of ASD was consistent with
the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders,
Fourth Edition, Text Revision [DSM-IV-TR] criteria [70], and
classiﬁcation of either autism or Asperger’s was made by a
clinician based on the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule
[ADOS] [71] and Autism Diagnostic interview-Revised [ADI-
R] [72].
evidence_spans.claim: ASD diagnosis was based on DSM-IV-TR criteria with ADOS and ADI-R used for clinical classification.

evidence_spans.text:
each rs-
fMRI image was partitioned into 200 (for ADHD, AD, and ASD)
or 125 (for PTSD/PCS) functionally homogenous regions of
interests (ROIs) using spatially constrained spectral clustering
[cc200 template] [76].
evidence_spans.claim: ASD rs-fMRI data were parcellated with the 200-region CC200 template.

evidence_spans.text:
Site-speciﬁc analysis was applied on the ADHD dataset. We
could not apply this analysis on ASD dataset since there was only
one site that had enough samples for HC and disease subgroups
evidence_spans.claim: No site-specific/leave-site-out analysis was possible for ASD because only one site had enough samples per group.

evidence_spans.text:
TABLE 9 | Peak similarity (highlighted), corresponding number of features, and number of clusters obtained using SFR, SFS, and GA with different clustering methods for
ASD dataset.
evidence_spans.claim: Table 9 reports peak similarity between clinical-diagnostic, phenotypic and connectivity-based clusters for ASD across feature-selection and clustering methods.
For ASD, genetic-algorithm feature selection with hierarchical clustering gave the highest clinical-diagnosis-vs-connectivity cluster similarity (89.20%), using 101 features and 3 clusters.

evidence_spans.text:
For ADHD and AD, highest similarity
was achieved between connectivity and phenotypic clusters, whereas for ASD
and PTSD/PCS, highest similarity was achieved between connectivity and clinical
diagnostic clusters.
evidence_spans.claim: For ASD, connectivity-based clusters corresponded most closely to clinical diagnostic groups (rather than to phenotypic clusters).

evidence_spans.text:
Data and source code
used in this work is publicly available at https://github.com/xinyuzhao/identiﬁcation-of
-brain-based-disorders.git.
evidence_spans.claim: Source code for the analysis pipeline is publicly released on GitHub.

assessments.support: N and diagnostic subgroup composition given (256 HC, 166 autism, 32 Asperger’s), with PDD-NOS explicitly excluded to reduce imbalance.
Seven contributing sites named; phenotypic variables (FIQ, VIQ, PIQ, ADI-R and ADOS subscores) listed in Table 3.
CC200 (200-ROI) parcellation is named, but preprocessing detail is deferred to an unavailable "Supplementary Material: Data Acquisition and Preprocessing".
DSM-IV-TR criteria with ADOS and ADI-R clinician classification; HC screened by self-report history questionnaire.
Site is identified (7 sites) but motion/QC is not addressed in the available text; no age/sex covariate handling described for ASD.
No site-specific or leave-site-out analysis was possible for ASD ("only one site that had enough samples"), so pooled clusters are not tested for site confounding.
Static and dynamic functional/effective connectivity measures computed from the CC200 parcellation are used as clustering features.

Peak cluster-similarity percentages are reported across feature-selection/clustering method combinations without a stated multiple-comparisons correction or significance test for the similarity values themselves.

risk_of_bias.summary: Cohort composition, sites and diagnosis source are clearly reported, and the CC200 atlas is named, but preprocessing detail is deferred to an unavailable supplement, no site-specific/leave-site-out check was possible for ASD due to sample distribution across sites, and the significance of the reported cluster-similarity percentages is not statistically qualified.

charting.title: Investigating the Correspondence of Clinical Diagnostic Grouping With Underlying Neurobiological and Phenotypic Clusters Using Unsupervised Machine Learning
charting.journal_conference: Frontiers in Applied Mathematics and Statistics
charting.disorder_diagnosis: Autism / Asperger’s (ASD) vs healthy control (HC); PDD-NOS excluded
charting.diagnosis_assessment: DSM-IV-TR criteria; clinician classification via ADOS and ADI-R
charting.comorbidities_included_excluded: HC screened by self-report history questionnaire to rule out ASD, ADHD, or Tourette's Disorder
charting.severity_levels: ADOS Total, Communication and Social subscores; ADI-R Social, Verbal, RRB and Onset subscores used as phenotypic variables
charting.dataset_openly_available: Yes — analysis source code publicly released on GitHub (https://github.com/xinyuzhao/identification-of-brain-based-disorders.git)
charting.feature_types: functional and effective connectivity (static and dynamic)
charting.specific_features: Static/dynamic functional and effective connectivity among 200 CC200 ROIs, with genetic-algorithm-based feature selection
charting.feature_extraction_tools: CC200 atlas (spatially constrained spectral clustering parcellation); preprocessing pipeline details deferred to an unavailable supplement
charting.importance_method: Genetic algorithm (GA) feature selection maximizing cluster similarity, compared against sequential forward selection (SFS) and an in-house SFR method
charting.model_category: Unsupervised clustering (density peak clustering, OPTICS, hierarchical clustering) with GA-based feature selection
charting.specific_algorithms: Density Peak Clustering (DPC), OPTICS, hierarchical clustering; feature selection via GA, SFS, and SFR
charting.validation_methodology: No cross-validation during clustering (explicitly stated); cluster-to-diagnosis/phenotype correspondence evaluated via similarity percentage, not a held-out classification test
charting.performance_metrics: Cluster similarity percentage (clinical diagnosis vs connectivity-based clusters, and vs phenotypic clusters)
charting.key_performance_results: For ASD, GA feature selection with hierarchical clustering gave the highest similarity (89.20%, 101 features, 3 clusters) between clinical-diagnosis clusters and connectivity-based clusters, exceeding the similarity to phenotypic clusters
charting.summary_key_findings: Using genetic-algorithm feature selection and unsupervised clustering of ABIDE rs-fMRI connectivity (CC200 atlas), ASD connectivity-based clusters corresponded most closely to the clinical diagnostic grouping (peak similarity 89.20% with hierarchical clustering), in contrast to ADHD and AD where connectivity better matched phenotypic clusters; no site-specific robustness check was possible for ASD due to sample distribution across the seven contributing sites.
charting.reviewer_notes: This paper studies four disorders (ADNI/AD, ADHD-200, ABIDE/ASD, in-house PTSD/PCS); only the ABIDE/ASD-specific content is charted here. The study design is an unsupervised clustering/correspondence analysis rather than a classical group-difference statistical test or a held-out predictive evaluation; charted as associational because no train/test classification performance is reported.

narrative_row.study_design_sample_dataset: Associational, unsupervised-clustering correspondence analysis; ABIDE (consistent with ABIDE I), 7 sites, 454 subjects with complete phenotypic data (256 HC, 166 autism, 32 Asperger’s; PDD-NOS excluded)
narrative_row.methods: rs-fMRI parcellated into 200 CC200 ROIs; static/dynamic functional and effective connectivity features selected via a genetic algorithm (compared against SFS and an in-house SFR method) to maximize similarity between connectivity-derived clusters (density peak clustering, OPTICS, hierarchical clustering) and clinical diagnosis or phenotypic groupings; no cross-validation during clustering.
narrative_row.outcomes: For ASD, connectivity-based clusters matched the clinical diagnostic grouping better than the phenotypic grouping, with a peak similarity of 89.20% (GA feature selection, hierarchical clustering, 101 features, 3 clusters); no site-specific robustness check was possible for ASD because only one site had sufficient samples per group.
narrative_row.key_limitations: Preprocessing pipeline and motion/QC details deferred to an unavailable supplement; no site handling/leave-site-out evaluation for the pooled multi-site ASD analysis; no cross-validation, so similarity values reflect in-sample correspondence rather than held-out predictive performance.
narrative_row.relevance_notes: Provides an ABIDE I cohort definition (454 subjects, 7 sites) and a connectivity-to-diagnosis correspondence finding (89.20% peak similarity) relevant to characterising how well unsupervised connectivity clusters recover clinical ASD groupings.
